summary:
Visitors stand under the United States federal framework in Hawaii as in every state. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 has required federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F from the supporting documents submitted, and passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, some stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

A separate entry exposure applies to trans athletes. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas and flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'; an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening can disclose status involuntarily. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening that matches one's presentation.

Hawaii's own standing is at the protective end of the national range. A national legal-risk assessment dated 13 July 2026, built from a rubric covering thousands of tracked anti-trans bills including youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the end of legal recognition, places Hawaii in the fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier, whose laws are described as having gone beyond minimum safeguards for trans rights.

Healthcare access is the second Hawaii-specific finding. The Movement Advancement Project's Transgender Healthcare Equality Map, with data as of 27 September 2026, lists Hawaii as a state holding a shield law or executive order. The shield protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care that is legal here was banned in the patient's home state, which is directly relevant to a visitor travelling from a ban state for treatment.
tangentialFactors:
The national range of exposure is wide, and a visitor's experience outside Hawaii can differ sharply. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright bans on facility use by gender identity, and trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances; twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement has occurred: in April 2025 a trans student who announced an intention to break the law and used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol was arrested and handcuffed, identified by civil-rights attorneys as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Identity documents are the fastest-moving restrictive area. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers, with rights groups describing the statute as a template other legislatures are following. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out state by state which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes and under what conditions.

The July 2026 assessment's worst-law tier supplies the contrast: one state carries up to five-year prison terms for the conduct it criminalises, and another maintains an arrest policy for gender-identity bathroom use. The same assessment's predecessor processes identified Idaho on 13 July 2026 as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated, and recorded that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures.

Shield coverage nationally is limited to sixteen states and the District of Columbia, covering 38% of trans people aged 13 and over, while thirty-two states and five territories, 56%, hold none; youth-care bans are tracked on the same map, some permanently blocked by courts.

Foreign governments have responded to the federal document and data rules. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States, advisories that followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.
localsOnly:
For residents, the shield law listed for Hawaii as of 27 September 2026 operates at the point of care: it shields patients and providers from civil or criminal charges arising from treatment that is lawful in Hawaii but prohibited in the patient's home state. Residents returning from care obtained elsewhere, and providers treating out-of-state patients, sit inside that protection.

Hawaii's placement in the fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier rests on a rubric that scores jurisdictions across youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the withdrawal of legal recognition. The tier contains fifteen named states alongside Hawaii, and its laws are characterised as having gone above and beyond the baseline in safeguarding trans rights.

Residents remain bound by the federal document regime for passports regardless of state-level standing: new applications are processed only as M or F from the supporting documents submitted, the X marker is no longer issued, and previously issued X-marker passports stay valid until expiry. Name and gender change sequences against federal records are documented in Lambda Legal's guidance.

Out-of-state legal action against Hawaii healthcare is the specific risk the shield law addresses, while thirty-two states and five territories nationally provide no equivalent protection for their own residents.
